key_concept: Frogs, like other anamniotes (fishes and amphibians), have 10 pairs of cranial nerves, while amniotes (reptiles, birds, mammals) have 12 pairs.
steps: Cranial nerves arise directly from the brain, unlike spinal nerves, which arise from the spinal cord.
The NCERT frog chapter states that 10 pairs of cranial nerves arise from the frog's brain.
These 10 pairs are: olfactory (I), optic (II), oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), auditory (VIII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X).
Nerves XI (spinal accessory) and XII (hypoglossal) are not counted as cranial nerves in anamniotes such as frogs.
Therefore, the frog has 10 pairs of cranial nerves, which matches option (3) and the official key.
why_not_others: Option (4), 12 pairs, is the count for reptiles, birds and mammals, including humans, and does not apply to frogs. Options (1) 6 and (2) 9 do not match the cranial nerve count of any vertebrate group.
common_trap: Students carry over the human figure of 12 pairs of cranial nerves and apply it to the frog.
time_saving_tip: Recall the rule: anamniotes (fishes and amphibians) have 10 pairs of cranial nerves, and amniotes have 12 pairs.
